title: Buying Versus Leasing
summary: Compare buying, financing and leasing over the same five years, then decide with the end position in view.
subtitle: Choose the contract that fits the driver, not the payment that photographs well

blocks.text: Two identical vehicles can leave the same dealership with completely different financial futures. The cup holders are standard; the consequences are optional extras.

This lesson compares paying cash, financing, leasing and a possible lease buyout over the same stretch of time. You will look beyond the monthly payment to the negotiated price, borrowing cost, kilometres, insurance and maintenance. You will also weigh what you must do when the lease ends and what you own or owe at the end. There is no universal winner. The useful answer depends on the driver, the contract and the written quote.
FCAC tells car shoppers to compare total cost, not only the payment or interest rate. A smaller payment can just mean a longer loan or a different end position.

items.title: “Leasing is always cheaper because the monthly payment is lower.”
items.text: A lease payment buys use for a set term, not automatic ownership. Compare the same number of years and include amounts due at signing, taxes, fees, kilometres, wear, buyout or return costs and what the vehicle is worth at the end.

blocks.text: A lower monthly payment can hide a longer loan or a completely different ending.
blocks.detail: Answering the same seven questions for every option is what stops one contract from looking cheaper than it turns out to be.
blocks.extra: The seven-number demand starts now, before any payment gets discussed.

sections.title: Make Every Option Answer the Same Questions

blocks.text: The dealer does not have to show the lowest available interest rate. FCAC recommends getting quotes from more than one dealer and lender and comparing rate, fees, amount financed, payment schedule and term.

items.text: Negotiated vehicle price before the payment discussion.
Down payment, trade-in credit or total amount due at signing.
Annual interest rate, lease rate and every financing charge.
Term, payment frequency and total scheduled payments.
Taxes, admin fees, acquisition and disposition fees, and optional products.
Lease kilometre limit, excess-kilometre charge, wear rules and how an early exit is priced.
What the vehicle is likely worth and what you still owe, or the lease buyout price, at the comparison date.

blocks.text: FCAC describes 72 months or more as a long-term car loan. A longer term may lower the payment while raising interest and the time you may owe more than the vehicle is worth.

items.title: “Buying is always smarter because ownership automatically creates value.”
items.text: Ownership can suit a long holding period, but the vehicle still loses value and needs insurance, maintenance and repairs. Buying only works when the price, the loan and the vehicle fit the household.

blocks.text: FCAC: Shopping around for auto financing

sections.title: Zoe, Liam and the Identical-SUV Problem

paragraphs: Cousins Zoe Singh and Liam O’Connor visit an Edmonton dealership on the same Saturday. Both like the same compact SUV. Zoe drives about 12,000 kilometres a year to an office. She expects to change vehicles after four years. Liam runs a renovation business and drives closer to 32,000 kilometres. He plans to keep his next vehicle until it develops strong opinions about winter.

The salesperson offers a lease with a low monthly payment and a seven-year loan with a slightly higher one. Both cousins reach for the lower number. Zoe has not asked about the kilometre limit. Liam has not noticed that the loan will outlast his repair budget. The monthly payment has walked in wearing a tiny cape, ready to save everyone from arithmetic.

Then they stop and build separate Five-Year Mobility Decision Boards. Zoe asks for the lease disclosure, the yearly kilometre limit, the excess charge, the amount due at signing and the buyout price. She adds insurance and a reserve for return costs. Liam gets written quotes from the dealer and his credit union. He cuts the extras he does not need and prices a shorter loan on a cheaper model.

The boards surprise them both. Zoe’s lease only works with a kilometre limit that matches her real driving, so she picks one and sets aside a return reserve. Liam’s surprise is bigger. The seven-year loan fails his test, and so does the new model. He chooses a cheaper used vehicle with a shorter loan, no kilometre limit and room in the budget for repairs.

Before signing, each checks the disclosure, the deposit terms, the insurance price and the provincial dealer rules. Five years later, Zoe returns her vehicle within the agreed conditions. Liam still owns his and still uses it for work. Neither contract won. They were not the same driver, so they did not pick the same contract. Once kilometres, time and the ending got a seat at the table, the choice was clear.

blocks.text: The same lease can suit a low-kilometre driver and punish a high-kilometre one. Labels do not decide fit. Your habits and the contract terms do.
Zoe and Liam compared written quotes over the same five years, priced the risks each driver created and recorded the end position before choosing.
Zoe and Liam left the same dealership with two different contracts, on purpose.
blocks.detail: Pausing to build a five-year board instead of comparing payments is what let two different drivers find two different right answers.
blocks.extra: Run the studio yourself next, before you sign anything.

sections.title: Run the Studio Before You Sign

items.title: Define the job
items.text: Record yearly kilometres, passengers, cargo, winter use, work use and how long you will keep it. A contract cannot fit needs that were never written down.

items.title: Separate price from payment
items.text: Negotiate or compare the vehicle price before term length, a trade-in or optional products blur the total.

items.title: Match the time horizon
items.text: Use the same number of months for every option. Add all cash paid and subtract a realistic end value. Do not compare a three-year lease with five years of ownership and declare victory.

items.title: Stress-test the exit
items.text: Ask what happens after job loss, a move, extra kilometres, heavy wear, an insurance write-off, early payout or negative equity.

items.title: Verify before signing
items.text: Read the disclosure and contract, keep copies and check provincial or territorial rules. In most jurisdictions there is no general cooling-off period for car loans or leases.

blocks.text: Most provinces and territories require lease-cost disclosure. Vehicle sales, deposits, dealer conduct and cancellation rights are set by each province or territory.
A proper five-year comparison ends with a position: vehicle owned, loan balance left, lease returned, return charges due or buyout available. ‘Payment finished’ is not a full ending.

items.title: “I can sign today and cancel tomorrow if I change my mind.”
items.text: In most provinces and territories, car loan and lease agreements do not have a general cooling-off period. Check deposit and cancellation terms before signing or paying.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why must buying and leasing be compared over the same time horizon?
items.detail: Then all cash paid and the end position are compared fairly.

items.title: What does negative equity mean?
items.detail: The vehicle is worth less than the remaining loan balance.

items.title: Which lease terms can make high or unpredictable driving expensive?
items.detail: Kilometre allowances, excess-kilometre charges, wear standards and early-exit terms.

items.title: Why request financing quotes from more than one source?
items.detail: The dealer need not show you the lowest rate. Several written quotes reveal differences in rate, fees, term and total cost.

items.title: What should be verified before paying a deposit or signing?
items.detail: The disclosure, the cancellation and deposit terms, the insurance cost, what the contract requires and your province’s or territory’s rules.

sections.title: Your Action: Five-Year Mobility Decision Board

blocks.text: Use written quotes and short references only. Mark estimates clearly, keep the original disclosures and never record banking passwords or full account numbers here.
The strongest vehicle decision fits in one sentence: this option fits my kilometres, how long I will keep it, the total cost, the risk I can carry and how I want it to end.
Compare the whole road, not just the monthly payment.
blocks.detail: Use the same time horizon, price the contract risks and record what you will own or owe at the end. The best option is the one that fits your real driving and financial capacity.

items.title: Depreciation
items.text: The decline in a vehicle’s market value over time.

items.title: Negative equity
items.text: A situation where the vehicle is worth less than the remaining loan balance.

items.title: Lease buyout
items.text: The price and steps for buying the leased vehicle, as set out in the agreement.

items.title: Residual or end value
items.text: What a vehicle is expected, or contractually set, to be worth at the end of a period.

items.title: Disclosure statement
items.text: A document showing key borrowing or lease costs and duties before you finalize the agreement.

items.title: Cooling-off period
items.text: A legal period when you can cancel certain contracts. It generally does not apply to car loans or leases in most of Canada.

quiz.question: True or False: “Leasing is always cheaper because the monthly payment is lower.”

questions: What will the vehicle do for you? Write your yearly kilometres and any cargo, winter or work needs.
How long will you realistically keep it?
Which quotes will you compare on the same date: cash, loan or lease? For each, write the price, the rate, the term and the total of all payments.
What will it cost to run for five years? Estimate insurance, fuel, maintenance and a repair reserve.
Where will you stand in year five? Write what the vehicle is worth and what you owe, or the lease return and buyout position.
What is your decision, and which risk did you test: kilometres, wear, negative equity or early exit? Add your no-pressure deadline.
